faults.where: title "Ghooma Hua Tile", round title "Tile Challenge", frame [[6,1],[9,3],[6,5],[3,3]]
faults.detail: The mix-up is 'a tilted square corner is not a right angle'. The drawn 'turned tile' is a rhombus with sides (3,2) and (-3,2): dot product -9+4 = -5, so its corners are NOT right angles. A child holding the belief ('a diamond-turned tile has no right angles') is never shown wrong; the piece shows a tilted tile that indeed has no right angle, which reinforces the mix-up rather than challenging it.

faults.where: title "Ghooma Hua Tile" / "Tile Challenge" vs frame [[6,1],[9,3],[6,5],[3,3]]
faults.detail: The words call the shape a turned (square) tile, but the drawn shape is a non-square rhombus (diagonals 4 and 6 units, corners not 90 degrees); a square tile turned like a diamond would have equal diagonals. Words disagree with the picture.

faults.where: screen bill card (p412 and l1366) vs spec rounds[0].customers[0].items[0]
faults.detail: Spec has "name": "Soap", "price": 50, "qty": 1, but the screen shows "Soap 1 × ₹0.50". The price shown disagrees with the spec, so the child is billed 50 paise for an item the engine prices at 50.

faults.where: spec rounds[0] (mode "pay", one customer, one item "Soap" price 50 qty 1)
faults.detail: The target mix-up is "Lines up numbers of different lengths from the left, so digits end up in the wrong places" (for example 3256 + 48). The only round bills one item of 50 with nothing to add, so there are no numbers of different lengths to line up. A child holding the mix-up would not go wrong here.
The topic is adding and subtracting 4-digit numbers (cards: 2345 + 1432, 5642 − 2318, 3256 + 48). A single ₹50 (or ₹0.50) soap with no sum does not practise column addition or subtraction.

faults.where: spec.rounds[0]: rule "multiple", a 6, lo 2, hi 60, title "6 ke groups", screen "6 Ke guna"
faults.detail: The mix-up is "Treats the × sign as +, so 6 × 4 is worked out as 6 + 4" (signs: "Says 3 × 5 = 8"). The round only asks the child to pick multiples of 6 from random numbers 2-60. No × expression appears, and nothing places the sum-trap values (6+k, such as 10 = 6+4) as decoys on purpose. A child who reads × as + can still find multiples of 6 by skip-counting (repeated addition), so the round does not show that child where the belief goes wrong. The 10 on the first screen is only a random draw (seed 17), not a designed trap.

notes: I could not tell from one first-screen frame and seed 17 which numbers appear later, so I did not count the distractor set as a separate fault. strings.runDone "Run done" is a short English phrase in a Hinglish piece. It is not a full sentence and it is not on the first screen, so I did not count it.

faults.detail: The mix-up is "Thinks 2/4 is more than 1/2 because there are more pieces", which is about comparing. This round asks the child to subtract 2/4 from 1/2 ("ghatao", answer 0). It does not ask the child to compare or to say which is more, so it never tests the point where the belief goes wrong. A child who believes 2/4 > 1/2 is not caught. The target's own rule says "a round aimed at a comparing mix-up compares, never adds", and a subtract operation is the same kind of fault.

faults.where: rounds[0] "op": "-" in topic c5-maths-ch02-t03 (equivalent fractions: cards "1/3 = ?/6", "3/4 = 9/?")
faults.detail: The topic practises equivalent fractions: finding the matching numerator or denominator, or saying whether two fractions are equal. Subtracting fractions is a different skill. The tools on screen ("kaato" stepper at 1 and a "dhalo" button) set up a cut-and-pour subtraction, not a check of whether the two are equal.

faults.where: waves[0], waves[1] (items [90,90,90,90]); screen: base arm fixed flat at '0°'
faults.detail: The mix-up is that only an 'L'-position right angle (one arm flat, one upright) counts. Every 90° round is drawn from a fixed horizontal base arm at 0°, so each right angle the child makes is the upright L. No round shows a tilted right angle, so the piece never reaches the point where the belief goes wrong. It only practises the L position the child already accepts.

faults.where: waves[1].sub: "Page ko ghuma kar bhi dekho"
faults.detail: This tells the child to turn the page to look. That is one of the mix-up's own listed signs ('Turns the page before deciding the type'), so the hint reinforces the wrong habit instead of showing that the angle stays 90° whichever way it faces.

faults.where: rounds[0]: title "Kone sajao", sub "Dono kone dhyaan se banao", challenges deg 35 and deg 145
faults.detail: The child is told both angles outright ("Kona 35°", then 145°) and only builds each one separately. Nothing says or shows that the two angles form a linear pair on a straight line, and the child never has to work out the partner angle. A child who believes a linear pair adds to 90° would build 35° and 145° just as easily, so the piece never reaches the point where that belief goes wrong (for example by answering 55° for the partner of 35°).
Misspelt. The Hindi word for isosceles is "Samdvibahu" (bahu = side), not "Samdvipahu".
The buttons sit on top of the rightmost column of the dot grid (x≈1159, the middle rows), so some grid points are partly covered. This overlaps the board the child builds on.

notes: The spec does not say whether the engine draws the 145° angle on the same arm as the 35° angle to make a linear pair. The first screen shows only the 35° challenge and an empty dot grid.

faults.detail: The target mix-up is 'Thinks lines are parallel only if they are the same length'. The given line is drawn edge to edge across the whole board (both screenshots), and the child draws a line of any length through the point. A child holding the belief can simply draw a line and be marked right; nothing asks them to accept a short and a long segment as parallel, so the belief never goes wrong on screen.
The sub-title promises segments of different lengths, but the picture shows the given line as a full-width line across the board (not a segment of any length), so the words disagree with the picture.
